chapters.title: Calcutta, 1881
chapters.src: Great Master 5.8a; Eastern & Western Disciples ch. 8
lines: Calcutta, eighteen eighty-one. A college student named Narendranath is reading Kant.
Kant tells him something unsettling: reason cannot see past its own walls.
Years later, as Swami Vivekananda, he would say the sages of India had found that wall long before.
And they had looked for a way through it.

chapters.title: What does not change
chapters.src: The Reality and the Shadow (CW vol. 8)
lines: The soul, he said, is always looking for something that does not change.
Wealth comes and goes. Ambition is fed, and is hungry again.
Everything we can grasp rises and falls, like a wave.
Religion, for him, was the search for what lies beneath the waves.

chapters.title: Kant's discovery
chapters.src: Inspired Talks, July 14, 1895; The Reality and the Shadow
lines: Here is the discovery he credited to Kant.
Time, space and causation are not things out there. They are modes of thought.
Every picture the mind makes is projected through these three.
Vedanta, he said, taught this ages ago, and called it Maya.
Not a product of thought, but the groundwork of all human thought.

chapters.title: X plus mind
lines: Look at a wall. Light reaches the eye, but you do not see the wall until the mind reacts.
Try it here. No triangle has been drawn on this card.
Your mind supplies every edge.
So the world we see is the real world, call it X, plus mind.
A blind man knows the world by touch and sound. Give us an electric sense, and the world would change again.
Each mind brings its own world. X remains unchanged.

chapters.title: Y plus mind
lines: Now turn inward. The self we feel is also seen through the mind.
Call the real self Y. What we know is Y plus mind.
Kant, he said, was the first to arrive at this analysis of mind. The Vedas had stated it long ago.
But X and Y are both beyond time, and time is what makes difference.
So they must be one. Seen outside, we call it the world. Seen inside, the Self.

chapters.title: Rope or snake
lines: Then are there two worlds, a real one hidden behind a false one?
No. At dusk, a man sees a snake on the path.
Someone brings a lamp. It was a rope.
He never saw both. Seen through the senses, the world is phenomenal. It was the real all along.

chapters.title: Will lives in time
lines: Schopenhauer said the world is will.
Vivekananda disagreed. Will needs a stimulus from outside. It is a compound, as much as a wall is.
And take Kant's analysis: one cannot will without willing in time.
Whatever lives inside time cannot be the Absolute.

chapters.title: Bay, strait, inlet
chapters.src: The Reality and the Shadow (CW vol. 8)
lines: My reality, nature's, and God's, he said, are the same. Only the form differs.
The shore shapes the ocean into a bay, a strait, an inlet.
Take away the shaping force, and all is ocean again.

chapters.title: The dead wall
chapters.src: Raja-Yoga, Introduction; Vedantism (Khetri); Buddhism and Vedanta
lines: Kant, he said, proved beyond doubt that we cannot get past the tremendous dead wall called reason.
That is exactly where Indian thought takes its stand.
The sages asked nature: do you know what the soul is? Nature answered, no.
So they turned inward, and struck out everything that could be seen. Neti, neti. Not this, not this.
When every appearance has been negated, whatever remains, that is It.

chapters.title: Two darknesses
lines: Is what lies beyond thought only the dull silence of a stone?
Light vibrating too slowly, we cannot see. Faster, it becomes light. Faster still, it is dark to us again.
The two darknesses are as different as the two poles.
The stone cannot reason. God does not need to.

chapters.title: Shankara first
chapters.src: The Vedanta in All Its Phases (CW vol. 3)
lines: Was this Kant's idea, carried East? Vivekananda said it was the other way round.
Shankara had identified time, space and causation with Maya, many centuries before.
He found the passages in Shankara's commentaries, and sent them to his friend, Professor Max Muller.

chapters.title: Stairs and roof
lines: Is the world unreal, then? A devotee once asked Ramakrishna.
While you climb, he said, you reason: the stairs are not the roof. Not this, not this.
Reach the roof, and you see the stairs are made of the same brick and lime.
God himself has become the universe. But reasoning alone will not show it.

chapters.title: Who bound us?
chapters.src: The Reality and the Shadow; Nivedita, The Master as I Saw Him
lines: Kant drew the wall. The Upanishads asked who stands behind it.
If we are bound, Vivekananda asked, who bound us? No power can bind the Infinite but Itself.
Which came first, the bird or the egg? Give it up. Escape from Maya.
And the student who studied Kant went looking for a man who had seen beyond the wall.
